items.title: Rosh Hashanah
items.what: For many Jewish families, Rosh Hashanah marks a new year and a time for reflection. Families observe it in different ways.
items.canada: Jewish communities have long histories and active cultural lives in BC.
items.fact: A new year does not begin in January in every calendar.
items.explore: Name a hope for the coming year. How could we support someone else’s hope?

items.title: Yom Kippur
items.what: For many Jewish people, Yom Kippur is a solemn time to reflect and seek forgiveness. Observance varies.
items.canada: Recognising important days helps Canadian schools respect family commitments.
items.fact: A solemn observance differs from a party or celebration.

items.title: Mid-Autumn: different family traditions
items.what: Some Chinese and Vietnamese families mark this season with gatherings and moon stories. Korean Chuseok has its own history and traditions around this season.
items.canada: Chinese, Vietnamese and Korean communities each contribute to Canadian life. Their traditions are not interchangeable.
items.fact: Sharing a season does not mean sharing one culture or celebration.

items.title: Orange Shirt Day / Truth and Reconciliation
items.what: Every child deserves care, family and respect. This day asks us to listen to residential school Survivors and keep learning about truth and responsibility.
items.canada: Residential schools harmed Indigenous children, families, languages and Nations in Canada. These histories carry responsibilities today.
items.fact: Phyllis Webstad’s orange shirt story is a specific person’s story. Indigenous peoples also have living cultures, governments and rights.
items.explore: Read the part of Phyllis Webstad’s story your teacher shares. Name a responsibility schools have towards children.
items.dateNote: National date: September 30. Surrey lists school recognition on September 29 in 2026; confirm school plans.

items.title: Canadian Islamic History Month
items.what: Muslim Canadians have many languages, family histories and ways of living. This month invites us to hear their stories.
items.canada: Canada recognises Islamic History Month in October. Muslim communities are part of Canada’s past and present.
items.fact: Muslim describes a religious identity, not one ethnicity or nationality.

items.title: Latin American Heritage Month
items.what: Latin American Canadian communities have roots in many places and include Indigenous, Black and other identities.
items.canada: October is Latin American Heritage Month in Canada.
items.fact: Spanish is not the only language spoken across Latin America.

items.title: Hindu Heritage Month
items.what: Hindu Canadians have many languages, traditions and family stories. There is no single way to be Hindu.
items.canada: November is Hindu Heritage Month in Canada. Include everyday community life as well as festivals.
items.fact: Hindi is a language; Hindu is a religious identity. They are not interchangeable.

items.title: Diwali / Deepavali
items.what: Many Hindu families celebrate Diwali or Deepavali. Jain traditions have their own meanings, and many Sikhs recognise Bandi Chhor Divas around this time.
items.canada: These occasions are part of contemporary life for many Canadian families, including in Surrey.
items.fact: Similar dates or lights do not make these traditions the same. Not every South Asian family observes them.
items.explore: What could we ask a community educator about how these occasions differ?

items.title: National Child Day
items.what: Children have rights to safety, learning, play and being heard. Rights belong to every child.
items.canada: Canada marks National Child Day on November 20.
items.fact: A right is not a prize for good behaviour.
items.explore: Choose one classroom routine. How does it help children use their rights? What could improve?

items.title: International Day of Persons with Disabilities
items.what: People move, communicate and learn in different ways. A barrier gets in the way of taking part.
items.canada: Disabled people and disability organisations in BC work for access and equal rights.
items.fact: Accessibility includes clear information, quiet spaces and communication choices, as well as ramps.
items.explore: Spot one barrier in a fictional school event. Change the event so more people can take part.

items.title: Hanukkah
items.what: Many Jewish families mark Hanukkah over eight nights. Traditions vary between families and communities.
items.canada: Jewish Canadian life includes many observances, languages, arts and everyday experiences.
items.fact: Hanukkah is not “Jewish Christmas”. These occasions have different histories and meanings.
items.explore: How can a school display name an occasion accurately without assuming everyone takes part?

items.title: Human Rights Day
items.what: Human rights protect people’s dignity. They matter in schools, homes and communities.
items.canada: Canadian museums and community organisations show how rights have been defended and denied.
items.fact: A written right does not always mean everyone can use it equally.

items.title: Tamil Heritage Month

items.fact: Tamil, Hindi and Telugu are distinct languages.

items.what: People with African roots belong to many distinct communities. Their lives include languages, art, families, work and community-building today.
items.canada: The Nigeria-Canada Association of BC and Surrey’s Yoruba association share local community voices.
items.fact: One Yoruba or Nigerian story cannot represent all Nigerians or all of Africa.
items.explore: Read one association’s description. Name a present-day community goal. What would another community’s voice add?
items.dateNote: World Day for African and Afrodescendant Culture, listed by Canadian Heritage. International observance, not an “African heritage month”.

items.title: International Holocaust Remembrance Day
items.what: The Holocaust was the persecution and murder of six million Jewish people by Nazi Germany and its collaborators. We learn from evidence and Survivors to remember people and recognise antisemitism.
items.canada: Vancouver Holocaust Education Centre preserves testimony and teaches Canadian connections, including exclusion of Jewish refugees.
items.fact: Jewish lives must be represented beyond persecution, including family, culture and life today.
items.explore: With teacher guidance, read a short, non-graphic life story. What do we learn about the person beyond what happened to them?

items.title: Black History Month in Canada
items.what: Black Canadians have shaped communities through art, work, care, organising and ideas. These stories belong in learning all year.
items.canada: Start with BC Black histories and community voices, then connect with other Black Canadian experiences.
items.fact: Black Canadian history is not simply US civil-rights history moved north. Canada has its own histories of exclusion and resistance.
items.explore: Choose a person or community from the BC Learning Centre. Name a goal, an action and what changed.
deeper: Listen to a story about a Black Canadian creator. Draw one contribution.
Connect a BC story to a place, a barrier and an action.

items.title: Lunar New Year: distinct traditions
items.what: Many Chinese families celebrate a new year at this time. Vietnamese Tết and Korean Seollal have their own names, meanings and traditions.
items.canada: Canadian communities carry, change and share traditions across generations.
items.fact: “Chinese” does not describe every East Asian community. Cantonese and Mandarin are also distinct language varieties.

items.dateNote: District planning date: February 6, 2027. Community events may span other days. Annual dates.

items.title: Ramadan
items.what: For many Muslims, Ramadan is a month of reflection, prayer, generosity and community. Some people fast; many children and others do not.
items.canada: Schools can offer flexible activities and respect family choices without singling anyone out.
items.fact: The Islamic calendar is lunar, so Ramadan moves through the Gregorian year. Appearance does not tell us who is fasting.
items.explore: Suggest a way to make an activity welcoming whether someone is fasting or not. No one needs to explain their choice.
items.dateNote: Anticipated: sunset February 7–March 8, 2027 in the district calendar. Moon sighting and community practice can shift dates.

items.title: International Mother Language Day
items.what: People may use several languages at home, at school or with friends. Languages carry stories, knowledge and relationships.
items.canada: Canada includes Indigenous languages, English, French, sign languages and languages brought through migration.

items.title: Canadian Multiculturalism Day
items.what: Canada holds many languages, histories, identities and ways of belonging. People can have several identities at once.
items.canada: June 27 invites reflection on who is heard and who still faces barriers in multicultural Canada.
items.fact: Cultural recognition does not replace Indigenous rights or action against discrimination.
items.explore: Look back at the year. Whose stories did we hear often? Whose voices should we seek next?

items.title: Emancipation Day in Canada
items.what: Emancipation means being freed from enslavement. This day remembers people who resisted slavery and worked for freedom.
items.canada: August 1 marks the 1834 coming into effect of the law abolishing slavery across much of the British Empire, including what is now Canada.
items.fact: Slavery existed in the lands now called Canada. Abolition did not end racism or create equal opportunity.
items.explore: What is the difference between a law changing and people having equal opportunities? Use a Black Canadian source.
items.dateNote: Summer observance. Preview in June or revisit in September; no summer assignment is expected.
